newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian state moves closer to euthanasia law.
newsitem.headline: Australian state moves closer to euthanasia law.

text.p: An Australian state has moved a step closer to introducing what would be only the world's second voluntary euthanasia law.

The South Australian parliament upper house voted 13-8 in favour of euthanasia legislation on Wednesday night, but the bill still faces another vote in the upper house and must then pass the lower house.
The world's first voluntary euthanasia law, in Australia's Northern Territory, lasted only nine months before being overturned by the country's national parliament in March.
Four people died using the Northern Territory law.

"It's the first step along a long road, but a very important step and the furthest any bill on euthanasia has ever gone other than the Northern Territory legislation," Anne Levy, the parliamentarian who presented the bill, said on Thursday.

"I am confident (it will be passed) as South Australia has a long tradition of leading Australia in social legislation," Levy told Reuters. Opinion polls show 75 percent of Australians support euthanasia.
Levy introduced the bill last November, before the Northern Territory law was overturned, dedicating it to the memory of her husband who died from cancer 20 years ago.
Under the Levy bill, adults of sound mind can request a lethal injection, either immediately if terminally ill or in the future should they become terminally ill.
Their request would need to be witnessed by a doctor, who would certify the patient did not suffer from a treatable clinical depression, and two witnesses.
Then 48 hours later a second doctor would certify the request and the injection could go ahead.
Anti-euthanasia activists said the South Australian legislation goes further than the territory law, which only allowed terminally ill patients to request assisted suicide.
The territory law also required three doctors' signatures, which proved difficult to attain and prevented some terminally ill patients from using the law before it was overturned.
Levy said her euthanasia bill would now be open to public debate before again being voted on by the parliament and she was happy to ammend its safety provisions.
"I don't want to be stubborn about it, I just want to get it passed so that people can have a choice," she said.
